title: Alabama Genetic Data Privacy Act
subtitle: Privacy requirements for direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies
summary: Alabama's Genetic Data Privacy Act took effect on October 1, 2024. It regulates businesses that directly solicit biological samples from consumers for genetic-testing products or services, as well as contractors handling data for those businesses.
legal_effects: Genetic testing companies must publish privacy notices and obtain initial express consent. Separate consent is required for each transfer or disclosure, uses beyond the requested service, and marketing. The act also provides access, deletion, and sample-destruction procedures, requires security and contractor confidentiality, and authorizes Attorney General enforcement.
plain_language: If you use a consumer genetic testing service covered by the act, the company must explain its data practices and ask before several uses or disclosures. You may access your genetic data, withdraw consent, and request data deletion or sample destruction through the act's procedures.
limitations: The act does not cover every holder of genetic information. Its exclusions include HIPAA-covered entities and business associates, health care providers, and certain noncommercial research conducted by higher education institutions.

title: Biological and neural data in health and fitness apps
subtitle: Proposed consent requirements for app-based data practices
summary: Alabama HB 263 did not become law. It would have regulated health and fitness applications that collect biological or neural data, including information generated by analyzing genetic or other biological properties to identify a person.
legal_effects: Covered app providers would have needed express consent before transferring or disclosing covered data, using it beyond a requested service, or using it for marketing. The Attorney General would have had exclusive enforcement authority, with a 45-day opportunity to cure and civil penalties of up to $3,000 per violation.
plain_language: The proposal would have let consumers limit how a covered health or fitness app reused or shared biological and neural data. Because the bill died, it created no new consent rights or penalties.
limitations: The proposal applied only to apps and data practices meeting its definitions. It excluded several categories, including certain regulated health information, research, insurance activities, deidentified data, security practices, and processing needed to provide a consumer-requested product or service.

title: Unlawful use of DNA
subtitle: Renewed proposal for criminal offenses involving nonconsensual DNA use
summary: Alabama HB 265 did not become law. It would have created first-, second-, and third-degree offenses for intentionally collecting, retaining, testing, disclosing, selling, or transferring another person's DNA sample or genetic data without express consent in specified circumstances.
legal_effects: The bill would have assigned different criminal penalties to unauthorized DNA sale or transfer, genetic testing or disclosure, and collection or retention. It would have used definitions from Alabama's Genetic Data Privacy Act.
plain_language: The proposal would have criminalized several intentional uses of another person's DNA without permission. Because it died, the proposed offenses and penalties never took effect.
limitations: Exceptions would have applied to specified legal process, law enforcement and forensic databases, and genetic testing companies complying with state law. The bill reached the House calendar but did not receive a House floor vote.

title: Alabama Personal Data Protection Act
subtitle: Comprehensive consumer-data protections that include genetic data
summary: Alabama enacted the Personal Data Protection Act in 2026, but its requirements do not take effect until May 1, 2027. The act treats genetic or biometric data processed to uniquely identify a person as sensitive data within a broader consumer privacy framework.
legal_effects: Businesses meeting the act's coverage thresholds must obtain consent before processing sensitive data. Covered controllers also have duties involving transparency, data minimization, security, consumer requests, targeted advertising, data sales, and certain profiling. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority.
plain_language: Beginning May 1, 2027, qualifying businesses must get consent before processing genetic data to uniquely identify a person. The act will also provide consumers with broader rights concerning personal data held by those businesses.
limitations: Coverage depends on business and data-processing thresholds. The act also has entity-level and data-level exemptions, including several for health care and federally regulated information, and generally excludes employment-context data from its definition of consumer.

title: Biological and neural data protections
subtitle: Proposed consent requirements for covered entities
summary: Alabama HB 436 did not become law. It would have regulated businesses that maintained, owned, or licensed biological or neural data, including data generated by analyzing genetic or other biological properties for identifying a person.
legal_effects: Covered businesses would have needed express consent before transferring or disclosing covered data, using it beyond a requested service, or using it for marketing. The Attorney General would have had exclusive enforcement authority, with an opportunity to cure and civil penalties of up to $3,000 per violation.
plain_language: The proposal would have let consumers limit how covered businesses reused or shared biological and neural data. Because the bill died in committee, it created no new consent rights or penalties.
limitations: Coverage would have depended on the bill's definitions. In particular, biological data had to be generated for identifying a person, and a covered entity had to maintain, own, or license biological or neural data. The introduced text did not contain the broad exclusions described in HB 263.

title: Genetic privacy and insurance protections
subtitle: Proposed consent, confidentiality, ownership, and insurance restrictions
summary: Alabama SB 58 did not become law. It would have required express consent for collecting, analyzing, using, retaining, or transferring DNA, declared DNA analysis results to be the individual's exclusive property and confidential, and restricted some insurer uses of genetic information.
legal_effects: The bill would have established criminal penalties for specified DNA collection, analysis, disclosure, and transfer without express consent. It also would have limited health, life, and long-term care insurers from requiring or using genetic information for specified eligibility, coverage, and premium decisions.
plain_language: The proposal would have given individuals more control over DNA samples and test results and limited some insurance uses. Because it died in committee, it created no new rights, restrictions, or penalties.
limitations: Exceptions would have applied to criminal investigations, court orders, medical care, regulated research, paternity matters, and other specified uses. Some insurance products were excluded, and insurers could still consider a medical diagnosis even when genetic information contributed to it.

title: Genetic Information Privacy Act
subtitle: Privacy requirements for direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies
summary: California's Genetic Information Privacy Act took effect on January 1, 2022. It regulates direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies that collect, use, maintain, or disclose genetic data collected or derived from a consumer or from the consumer's biological sample.
legal_effects: Covered companies must publish privacy notices, obtain separate express consent for listed uses and disclosures, provide access and deletion methods, and maintain reasonable security practices. After a qualifying consent revocation, a company must destroy the consumer's biological sample within 30 days.
plain_language: If you use a genetic testing company covered by the act, it must explain its data practices and ask separately before several uses or disclosures. You may access or delete your data and request sample destruction through the act's procedures.
limitations: The act excludes protected health information governed by HIPAA and medical information governed by California's Confidentiality of Medical Information Act. It also contains exceptions for specified research and other activities.

title: Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008
subtitle: Federal protections in health coverage and employment
summary: The Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008, or GINA, is a federal law that restricts how covered health insurers and employers may use genetic information when making health-coverage or employment decisions. Separate parts of the law govern health coverage and employment. Each part contains its own definitions, exceptions, effective dates, and enforcement rules.
legal_effects: Title I limits how covered health plans and insurers may request or use genetic information. Title II limits how covered employers and other employment entities may acquire, use, or disclose genetic information. Both titles contain exceptions and enforcement provisions.
plain_language: GINA protects genetic information in two main settings: health coverage and employment. It generally prevents covered health insurers and employers from using that information in certain decisions. It does not provide the same protections for life, disability, or long-term care insurance.
limitations: GINA does not apply to every organization, insurance product, or use of genetic information. Whether it applies depends on the organization, the decision being made, and any statutory exception. Review the current law or seek legal advice for a specific situation.

title: HIPAA Privacy Rule treatment of genetic information
subtitle: Genetic information as protected health information
summary: The 2013 HIPAA final rule made clear that genetic information is health information under the HIPAA Privacy Rule. It also prohibited most health plans covered by HIPAA from using or disclosing protected health information that is genetic information for underwriting.
legal_effects: The rule revised HIPAA definitions and barred most HIPAA-covered health plans from using or disclosing genetic information for underwriting. It took effect on March 26, 2013, with a September 23, 2013 compliance date.
plain_language: Identifiable genetic information held by a health plan, health care provider, or clearinghouse covered by HIPAA can be protected health information. The rule also limits how most covered health plans may use it for underwriting.
limitations: HIPAA does not apply to every organization that collects genetic information. Coverage depends on the organization, the information, and the activity. The underwriting prohibition does not apply to issuers of long-term care policies.

title: NIH Genomic Data Sharing Policy
subtitle: Expectations for sharing large-scale human and non-human genomic data
summary: The NIH Genomic Data Sharing Policy applies to NIH-funded research that generates large-scale human or non-human genomic data and to later research using those data. For covered awards and contracts, compliance with the approved data-sharing plan becomes a term and condition of funding.
legal_effects: Applicants must provide a basic genomic data-sharing plan. Before an award, institutions must provide a more detailed plan and certification that identifies consent-based data-use limits and whether human data should use unrestricted or controlled access.
plain_language: If an NIH-funded project falls within the policy, the investigators and their institution must plan how and when genomic data will be submitted and shared. Human data may use unrestricted or controlled access based on consent and institutional review.
limitations: This is a funding policy, not a statute that applies to every genomic research project. Requirements depend on the award, the data generated, participant consent, NIH institute or center guidance, and any approved exception.

title: Confidentiality of records of genetic tests
subtitle: Consent, confidentiality, and biological-sample requirements
summary: New York Civil Rights Law section 79-l generally requires written informed consent before a genetic test is performed and before results are disclosed. It also treats genetic-test records and results as confidential and regulates the retention, research use, and destruction of biological samples.
legal_effects: The person or organization ordering a genetic test must obtain written informed consent. Separate written consent is generally required to disclose results. Unless the tested person authorizes longer retention, the biological sample generally must be destroyed within 60 days after written results are provided to the tested person.
plain_language: In most covered situations, you must give written permission before a genetic test is performed or its results are shared. The law also limits how long a sample may be kept and when it may be used for research.
limitations: The section contains exceptions and special rules for court orders, specified public health programs, research, insurers, and other circumstances. Whether the consent, confidentiality, or destruction rules apply depends on the purpose of the test and the statutory exception at issue.
